items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: About 1920, Signorelli joined my band... Frankie stood with me from 1920, part of 1920, 21, and 22.

ctx.x: Well, we forgot about Lytel and Frankie Signorelli. About 1920, Signorelli joined my band. At that time they may have had a Memphis Five, but I never heard of them stopping the machine. Well, I had a little bit of friction with Roberson. He had promised the band a thousand dollars if I put Margie over. Well, I saw the plug of Margie for him, sang it for him, placed it on the record for him, and after he got his first statement, he didn't say anything. I asked him about what he was going to do to three of them.…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: I gave Robertson his two weeks notice and replaced him with Frank Signorelli.

ctx.x: Now what did people object to in the dance?

Well they said we had a sexual music that we were ruining the morals of the girls. They, people would get out there and they'd forget they were dancing, standing in one spot and starting moving around. In other words the great masters tried to move them. But they didn't succeed. I guess ours was like wine or good wine. When the people would get interested in our music. They'd stand there. Some of them would dance around. Stand there and they just moved themselves like worms. And many of the times we'd sneak off…

many of the places we had returning engagements. Through my files, you'll be able to see the office of jobs we had. And all the New Orleans boys was not working. And if I'd have had a thousand men that could play our music, I could have been a millionaire today because I had jobs for all of them. But there was none of them could fit the bill. In this one-night stands, we came back. And it was a tough job, riding all night to go to another place. For instance, you'd jump from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh. It was…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: he recorded with us in the latter part of our contact with the victim.

ctx.x: You asked me that I forgot to say who replaced Lytel and Signorelli. Two New York boys, they were both from Brooklyn. One was Artie Seboyg and the other was Henry Vanacella. He played the flam net and Vanacella played the piano. Now, each change I made, I didn't come to New Orleans. Although I was relegated in a dance hall.
What about Signer Running? You say he made some records.

Oh yes, he recorded with us in the latter part of our contact with the victim. The numbers offhand I can't tell you, but if you look through the files, you'll find out I have letters that I sent to this Brian Russ, and I tell him about the men who played on the recording.
